target.title: Silent Speech and Emotion Recognition from Vocal Tract Shape Dynamics in Real-Time MRI

entries.text: The authors claim this is the first study to recognize an entire spoken sentence from an individual's articulatory motions captured by rtMRI video.
entries.condition: Sentence-level recognition from an individual's vocal-tract rtMRI video.
entries.quote: To the best of our knowledge, this is the first study that demonstrates the recognition of entire spoken sentence based on an individual’s articulatory motions captured by rtMRI video.

entries.text: The authors claim a first end-to-end sentence-level rtMRI articulatory recognition framework jointly learns spatiotemporal visual features and sequential information.
entries.condition: rtMRI articulatory speech recognition; visual feature extraction and sequence modeling are learned together.
entries.quote:
believe, is the first end-to-end sentence-level articulatory speech
recognition2 framework for rtMRI data that simultaneously learns
spatiotemporal visual features and sequential information.

entries.text: The recognition frontend uses three STCNN layers for spatiotemporal feature extraction.
entries.condition: Variable-length vocal-tract video sequences are processed by the recognition frontend.
entries.quote:
The recognition model takes a sequence of 𝑇 frames as input to
process by 3 layers of spatiotemporal convolutions (STCNN) [9].

entries.text: Two Bi-GRUs feed a linear layer and softmax character outputs.
entries.condition: Sequence modeling module after the STCNN frontend.

entries.text: USC-TIMIT contains ten speakers, split by gender evenly; mean age is 28.7 years (SD 7.2).
entries.condition: USC-TIMIT 2D rtMRI vocal-tract videos; the speaker demographic description for the recognition corpus.
entries.quote: ten speakers (5 female and 5 male, M = 28.7 years, SD = 7.2)

entries.text: The training partition comprises 3,680 videos from eight speakers.
entries.condition: USC-TIMIT training set; the paper reports the split by speaker count.
entries.quote: a “training dataset” with 3,680 videos of eight speakers

entries.text: The testing partition comprises the remaining 920 videos from two speakers and is described as unseen data.
entries.condition: USC-TIMIT test set; remaining videos and speakers after the eight-speaker training partition.
entries.quote: a “testing dataset” with the remaining 920 videos of two speakers.

entries.text: Word-to-frame alignment uses a video frame rate of 23.18 frames per second.
entries.condition: USC-TIMIT word-level transcription aligned to rtMRI frame sequences by word duration multiplied by frame rate.
entries.quote: Hence, we estimated the number of frames by multiplying duration (second) of each word by video frame rate (23.18 frames/second) and aligned with its word-level transcription.

entries.text: Training labels originate from synchronized, time-aligned word-level transcriptions, which the authors align to the video frames using word duration and frame rate.
entries.condition: USC-TIMIT supervised training; frame count is estimated from each word's duration, not a separately described phoneme-level alignment.

entries.text: Horizontal mirroring augmented training data to 10,972 samples; both original and mirrored image sequences were trained on.
entries.condition: Augmented training partition; augmentation is a horizontal mirror of video frames.

entries.text: Each model input is fixed to 75 frames, approximately three seconds.
entries.condition: Input video sequence length for recognition model.
entries.quote: The number of frames was fixed to 75,∼3 seconds.

entries.text: Sequences longer than the fixed input length are truncated; shorter sequences are zero-padded.
entries.condition: All input clips are represented at the fixed 75-frame length.

entries.text: Batch size was explored from 16 to 256 and selected as 32.
entries.condition: Hyperparameter selection for the recognition model.

entries.text: Training steps per epoch were varied from 50 to 500 and fixed at 100 based on accuracy.
entries.condition: Hyperparameter selection for the recognition model.

entries.text: The end-to-end network is trained with Adam and batch size 32.
entries.condition: Recognition network training on augmented USC-TIMIT training samples.

entries.text: The recognition-model learning rate is 10^-3.
entries.condition: Adam training of the end-to-end recognition network.

entries.text: Dropout of 0.5 is applied after each max-pooling layer.
entries.condition: Recognition network convolutional frontend.

entries.text: Training the network with 10,972 samples took approximately 3.5 hours on an NVIDIA GeForce 1080Ti.
entries.condition: 10,972 augmented training samples; NVIDIA GeForce 1080Ti hardware (see t17b).

entries.text: The network is implemented with Keras/TensorFlow and trained using an NVIDIA GeForce 1080Ti GPU.
entries.condition: Hardware/software environment reported for recognition-network implementation.

entries.text: The emotion geometry analysis uses 56 productions per word across three non-neutral emotions from ten speakers, with two words analyzed.
entries.value: 56 per word per emotion; 10 speakers; 2 words; 3 emotions
entries.condition: USC-EMO-MRI-derived analysis of “clock” and “dock”; five male and five female speakers; happy, angry, and sad compared with neutral.
entries.quote: A total of 56 productions of each word as a function of emotion spoken by ten speakers (5 male and 5 female) were analyzed (56 productions× 2 words× 3 emotions).

entries.text: The authors introduce the Neutral Emotion Deviation Measure (NEDM) to quantify vocal-tract shape distortion relative to neutral emotion.
entries.condition: Cross-distance deviations from neutral, measured from the centroid to landmarks on upper and lower airway-tissue boundaries across vocal-tract subregions.

entries.text: NEDM is the summed absolute difference between emotion and neutral centroid-to-landmark distances, normalized by the corresponding neutral distances; Table 3 reports averages.
entries.condition: Computed separately by subregion and upper/lower boundary; neutral emotion is the reference.

entries.text: The vocal tract is analyzed in pharyngeal, velar/dorsal constriction, hard palate, and labial constriction regions, separately for upper and lower boundaries.
entries.condition: Airway-tissue boundary analysis uses four anatomically defined regions and two boundary traces.

entries.text: Emotion analysis uses semi-automatic MATLAB airway-tissue boundary segmentation, including lip/larynx tracking, boundary segmentation, pixel-sensitivity correction, noise suppression, and distance computation.
entries.condition: Semi-automatically constructed gridlines support automatic tracking and segmentation steps.

entries.text: The authors report greater NEDM deviation for lower than upper boundary subregions across emotions.
entries.condition: Emotion geometry results pooled across the analyzed words and gender groups.

entries.text: The authors report more distortion in velar/dorsal and hard-palate regions for high-arousal anger and happiness than for sadness.
entries.condition: NEDM geometry analysis of the analyzed word productions.

entries.text: For all emotions, female speakers show more noticeable changes across all analyzed regions.
entries.condition: Emotion analysis across five female and five male speakers.

entries.text: The authors conclude that vocal-tract subregion distortion is affected by both emotion and gender.
entries.condition: Emotion/gender analysis of two words across ten speakers.

entries.text: The authors report little variation by gender in the labial constriction region compared with other regions.
entries.condition: NEDM emotion-geometry analysis by gender.

entries.text: For anger, female speakers show more geometrical distortion in the pharyngeal and velar/dorsal regions than for happiness.
entries.condition: Emotion geometry comparison by gender and region.

entries.text: The authors report palatal constriction and release as more emphasized for happiness than anger.
entries.condition: Emotion-dependent vocal-tract movements.

entries.text: The authors state that the envisioned assistive and day-to-day applications are not yet technologically achievable in their work.
entries.condition: Potential computer interaction and communication uses, including people with speech disorders, muteness, or blindness.

entries.text: The authors expect recognition performance could improve with additional training data, citing prior deep-speech-recognition literature.
entries.condition: Future performance expectation; not measured as a data-scaling experiment in this paper.

questions.q: Do USC-TIMIT test speakers read the same sentences as the training speakers?
questions.answer: The target does not say (t96). Csapo 2020 states every USC-TIMIT speaker reads the same 460 MOCHA-TIMIT sentences (c13); 3,680/8 and 920/2 both equal 460 videos per speaker (inference). Answered by the writer from the named passages, no reader run needed.

questions.q: Does any earlier rtMRI work recognize continuous-speech sequences?
questions.answer: Katsamanis et al. 2011: HMM recognition of articulation-type sequences in 460 TIMIT utterances of one speaker, 49.4% accuracy over 10 random 95/5 splits (c8-c11). Answered by grep of the named passage.
